newsitem.title: CANADA: S&P raises Canadian debt rating outlook.
newsitem.headline: S&P raises Canadian debt rating outlook.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Monday it upgraded Canada's foreign currency debt rating outlook, citing declining government deficits which had put the country on a better financial footing.
But the debt rating agency said Canada still had too much debt to be reassigned the top triple-A rating it lost in 1992.

New York-based S&P upgraded the outlook on Canada's foreign currency rating to stable from negative. The agency also confirmed the foreign currency debt rating at AA+ and the local currency debt rating at AAA.

The foreign currency debt rating is placed on Canadian government bonds denominated in foreign currencies. While Canada does little borrowing in foreign currency bonds, the rating has a strong symbolic importance.
Canada lost its AAA foreign currency rating in October 1992 and the outlook was lowered to negative from stable in February 1995.

"The main reason (for the change in outlook) is the improved fiscal performance of the federal government, which has been quite successful in sticking to its deficit targets," said Valerie Blair, a director with Standard & Poor's in Toronto.
Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin last week delivered a market-friendly federal budget that held the line on spending and committed the government to further deficit cuts for the next two years.
Other factors prompting the change in the rating outlook included diminished reliance on foreign borrowing and reduced political uncertainty about Quebec's independence movement.
High debt was the main impediment to a full rating upgrade for Canada, S&P said.

The agency noted that the federal government's debt was about 75 percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1996/97 ending March 31. Total debt among Canada's various levels of government was about 100 percent of GDP.
